Analyses We ﬁt generalized estimating equations (GEEs) predicting Time 2 outcomes (adult words per minute and SPEAK scores) from the Time 1 counterparts. All models clustered observations by family to account for sibling pairs and used an exchangeable working correlation with robust (sandwich) standard errors. Follow-up models also included additional covariates as sensitivity checks and to examine potential independent effects on outcomes. Covariates included: hospital site; participating parent’s gender, age, and education level; whether this was their ﬁrst baby; infant’s assigned sex, age (GA, CA, and PMA), SBS and CAMEO scores, intubation and chemical paralysis status, presence of neurological/auditory concerns, and Time 1–Time 2 change in total visitor minutes. Finally, group-by-covariate interaction terms were added to examine whether intervention effects varied according to any demographic or clinical measure. Analyses were conducted in R using geepack for GEEs and emmeans for estimated marginal means and contrasts. Each analysis uses listwise deletion to only examine complete cases (ﬁnal N = 93 for SPEAK analyses, N = 90 for LENA analyses). Results for the SPEAK survey are reported as odds ratios (OR) and predicted mean scores, while results for the adult words are reported as a ratio of means (Intervention/Control) with corresponding percent differences. Signiﬁcant interactions for continuous variables are described and visualized via median-splits.

RESULTS Sample Complete participant demographics (infant and parent) are reported in Table 1. Ninety-two participants completed the entire study, while 8 (4 intervention, 4 control) did not complete all measures due to discharge/transfer to another unit or change in clinical status. See Fig. 2 for a CONSORT diagram of participation/ attrition. Parents who completed the questionnaires and intervention were primarily mothers (84%), but varied widely in age, race and ethnicity, and education level. Sixty-ﬁve percent of parents reported this was their ﬁrst child. At enrollment, infants (45% female) ranged in GA from 22.4 to 40.7 weeks, CA from 2 days–42.7 weeks and PMA from 31.0 to 68.7 weeks. Diagnoses varied widely, with 38% having neurological or auditory concerns, 26% were intubated, and 4% were chemically paralyzed. Most infants (69%) had an SBS score of 0, indicating they were awake and able to calm, and CAMEO scores ranged from 71-143, corresponding to levels II-V (where V is the highest level of care complexity) (Table 1). Two families in the control group were excluded from LENA analyses for having large differences ( > 3 SD)

in the number of family visitation minutes between Time 1 and Time 2. There were no signiﬁcant differences between intervention and control groups for any infant or parent demographic measures (all p > 0.2).

Intervention effects on parents’ knowledge of infant cognitive & language development Parents whose infants were assigned to the intervention group had higher Time 2 SPEAK scores (controlling for Time 1) compared to controls (OR = 2.79, 95% CI = 1.94–4.01, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3A). Speciﬁcally, the intervention group exhibited an estimated 7.6% increase, while the control group exhibited only a 0.8% increase. This result remained signiﬁcant after controlling for all parent and infant demographic measures (all p < 0.001). There was also a signiﬁcant independent effect of recruitment site, such that parents from the level III NICU scored higher on average than the parents from the level IV NICU (OR = 1.65, 95% CI = 1.12–2.41, p = 0.01). There were also a signiﬁcant interaction between group assignment and infants’ SBS scores (OR = 2.08, 95% CI = 1.37–3.15, p < 0.001), such that the intervention was most effective at increasing parents’ SPEAK scores when infants had higher SBS scores (i.e., were more awake; Fig. 3B). Speciﬁcally, when infants were awake (SBS ≥0), the intervention led to an estimated 13.8% score increase, while when the infant was sedated or unresponsive (SBS < 0), there was only a 7.6% increase.

Intervention effects on infants’ language environments Infants of parents who were assigned to the intervention group experienced more adult words per minute at Time 2 (controlling for Time 1) compared to those in the control group (OR = 1.43, 95% CI = 1.13–1.82, p = 0.004; Fig. 4A). Speciﬁcally, the intervention group exhibited an estimated 8.4% increase, while the control group exhibited an estimated decrease of 26.6%. This result remained signiﬁcant after controlling for all parent and infant demographic measures (all p < 0.04). There were also signiﬁcant interactions between group assignment and infant intubation status (OR = 1.72, 95% CI = 0.88–3.36, p = 0.01; Fig. 4B), parents’ education level (OR = 0.88, 95% CI = 0.80–0.98, p = 0.021; Fig. 4C), and participating parent gender (OR = 0.47, 95% CI = 0.23–0.94, p = 0.032); Fig. 4D. DISCUSSION In this randomized controlled trial, we found that a brief parental education program for NICU parents led to a signiﬁcant improvement in parents’ knowledge of infant cognitive and language development, as well as short term infant language exposure in the NICU, even after adjusting for sociodemographic factors known to affect language exposure. Given that infants who are hospitalized in the NICU are often at high risk of

neurocognitive delays, this intervention provides a highly feasible opportunity to maximize in-hospital language exposure and potentially improve infants’ neurodevelopment outcomes. While it was beyond the scope of this research to assess longer term outcomes, it helps lay the foundation for sustained language enrichment. Parents of infants hospitalized in the NICU are a particularly valuable target for this intervention, as it provides a practical, actionable skillset that has long-term beneﬁts for their child. In recent years, family integration in NICU care has been shown to improve parental mental health and infant health outcomes [34]. including long-term neurodevelopment. However, speciﬁc caregiving behaviors within the NICU targeting neurodevelopmental outcomes are vastly understudied. In-unit education has been shown to effectively promote several practical caregiving skills, including infant feeding, bathing, and administering medications [35, 36]. However, our prior investigation found that, given the social and medical complexity of a NICU hospitalization,

families often do not feel empowered or informed about the importance and logistics of speaking to their infants [20]. This leads these already high risk infants admitted to a NICU to have lower exposure to language and parental conversation, and therefore less auditory stimulation during a critical period of brain development. The educational intervention described in this study improved parental understanding of the importance of adult speech to infant cognition and language development, offering an accessible and targeted way for families to contribute to their infant’s development, and another method of family integration into NICU care. In older infants, the frequency of language exposure at home has been associated with improved cognition throughout childhood [37]. In the NICU, exposure to an increased number of adult words has also been shown to relate to better language development in the ﬁrst years of life [14]. Most efforts to increase infant language exposure in the NICU has been limited to playing audio-recordings of parental voices or parental reading interventions [21]. Recently, an intensive 6-week intervention for families of preterm infants in a level III NICU demonstrated increased infant language exposure in the NICU and long-term beneﬁts to children’s language development [22]. Our work builds on prior literature by demonstrating that a brief, accessible, and feasibly scalable intervention resulted in short term increased language exposure for infants in both level III and level IV NICUs—similar to that seen in prior intensive interventions—accompanied by improvements in parents’ knowledge of language and cognitive development that may inﬂuence their future, post-discharge interactions. Importantly, we also show that the intervention provided the greatest beneﬁts for the most at-risk infants, offering promising next steps toward mitigating established sociodemographic disparities in neonatal outcomes. Additionally, intervention effects on infants’ language exposure were greatest for infants who were intubated, and potentially for those who were chemically paralyzed, although this sub-sample was very small (n = 4) and ﬁndings may not be interpretable. This is consistent with ﬁndings from our prior qualitative study, in which we surveyed NICU families and providers about their views on communicating with infants in the NICU [20]. Parents noted their intimidation, lack of knowledge, and fear about communicating with acutely ill infants —especially when they were intubated and/or required other invasive equipment—often not knowing if their babies could hear them, if talking might cause more harm than good, or feeling like

they needed permission to interact and communicate. The present intervention likely provided families of acutely ill infants the conﬁdence to communicate with their infants, leading to the greatest increases in language exposure. On average, children whose parents have attained higher levels of education are exposed to more child directed speech than those whose parents had lower educational attainment, leading to higher lexical development through early childhood [38]. This effect is magniﬁed in children with high medical complexity, a risk factor for NICU graduates [39]. While the parent education level was overall high, the present intervention led to the greatest increases in infants’ language exposure when parents had lower educational attainment. This offers a concrete step toward improving equitable outcomes. This is especially notable given that other language-focused interventions in medical settings had effects limited to higher SES parents [40]. Additionally, the intervention was most effective when the father was the parent who participated. Note that this does not mean that fathers necessarily spoke more to their infants, because the LENA records all speech from all nearby adults when visitors are present, and we are unable to determine exactly who was speaking when. However, in families where the father was the participating parent, the father also spent more time at the bedside, compared to families where the mother was the participating parent, so it is plausible that the father’s speech did increase. A robust body of literature in typically developing infants ﬁnds that infants hear signiﬁcantly more speech from mothers than fathers [41, 42]. and this has also been found in the NICU setting [15, 43]. Fathers may be a particularly important source of language input in the NICU, especially if medical conditions limit a mother’s ability to interact. Thus, our ﬁndings suggest that interventions with fathers may be particularly effective at increasing the overall amount of speech infants are exposed to in the NICU. Importantly, the present intervention is highly scalable to other NICU settings. The curriculum consisted of freely available videos and handouts, together taking approximately 30 min to review. Parents generally enjoyed the curriculum and appreciated being provided with actions they could take immediately to support their infants’ development, which is important in settings where parents often feel like they have little control in their child’s outcomes [44]. Third, the LENA does not distinguish between infant directed speech and non-directed speech, such as nurses and parents talking to each other, or parents talking on the phone. However, since this percentage would not be

expected to consistently increase in the Time 2 compared to Time 1 LENA recording, and only in the intervention group, we do not expect this to alter to our ﬁndings. Fourth, because our study sample was predominantly White, non-Hispanic, and highly educated, it may limit assessment of the intervention’s impacts on parents from minoritized race and ethnicities and with lower educational attainment; however, initial ﬁndings suggest enhanced effects for families with lower education. Finally, while we demonstrate immediate intervention effects similar to those of longer, more intensive interventions, it is important to examine long-term effects on parent language practices and ultimately children’s linguistic and cognitive outcomes. There is a risk of intervention fade out [47]. in which the noted initial new behavior returns to baseline without reinforcement. More studies following knowledge retention and language behavior over a longer course duration are needed before conclusions can be drawn regarding long term effects.

CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the effectiveness of a brief, accessible, feasible educational intervention to improve the quantity and quality of parent-infant interaction in the NICU, with the greatest beneﬁt to infants at highest risk of neurocognitive delay. This intervention simultaneously empowers families to participate in their infant’s neurodevelopment while maximizing the prolonged NICU hospitalization to promote optimal language exposure for high-risk infants.
